implementation_notes: C++ expresses all five directly: abstract base classes with pure virtual functions for the abstraction, pure virtual destructors to keep the base polymorphic, deleted copy for non-substitutable value types, and templates (or C++20 concepts) for static dispatch where virtual cost is measurable. Pimpl is the classic C++ answer to hiding a change-prone implementation behind a stable header.
pitfalls: Forgetting the virtual destructor makes deleting through the base undefined behaviour.
Non-virtual public methods inherited from a concrete base break substitutability without any compiler warning.
Templates give static dispatch but freeze the implementation at the call site — that defeats runtime pluggability.
`override` omitted silently desynchronises the vtable after a signature change.
